dataset_family: Szeged-Columbia bilingual telephone speech sample: Memory Clinic, Dept of Psychiatry, University of Szeged (Hungarian, n=33: 20 HC/13 MCI) + Memory Disorders Center, NYSPI/Columbia (English, n=33: 19 HC/14 MCI); N=66; Szeged corpus family shared with P-59 (registry)
method_family: Phone-level ASR (DNN acoustic model, English TEDLium or Hungarian BEA) deriving temporal/hesitation speech parameters (articulation rate, tempo, silent and filled pauses) + SVM; speaker-wise nested leave-one-out CV
what_it_shows: A spontaneous monologue ('tell me about your previous day'; the PDF gives no duration, so the finder's 'one-minute' is not supported by it) was captured over a mobile-phone call and recorded by a call-recorder app, so no specialist hardware was used. It was interviewer-initiated, not self-administered. The MCI label is a clinical Petersen-criteria diagnosis. Under speaker-wise nested leave-one-out CV in 33 speakers per language, accuracy (computed at the equal-error-rate threshold) is 84.8% for English with all features (AUC 0.932). For Hungarian it is 90.9% with filled-pause features only (AUC 0.912; 0.923 with the English ASR). The Hungarian full feature set gives 75.8% (AUC 0.727), and the silent-pause subsets are near chance (AUC 0.519-0.531). There is no external validation and no head-to-head against a specialist instrument.
why: Gosztolya et al. 2021, Computer Speech & Language 69:101215. The PDF title and authors match the block (cross-lingual English/Hungarian MCI detection from temporal speech parameters; 66 eligible, 33 per language), and the DOI matches the map. The block has no Title/Authors fields but its content matches the PDF. Read in full; the reference list is omitted from the extract. TABLE A1: PARTLY. It shows a consumer device (a mobile phone with a call-recorder app, p.4) and a best-case standalone accuracy in the band (90.9%, Table 3 p.7). It is NOT self-administered: 'a second investigator called the subject on a mobile phone' and gave a standardised instruction (p.4). NARROWED WORDING: YES. Low-cost behavioural data captured without specialist hardware (a phone call) gives a best-case standalone accuracy of about 91% (Hungarian filled-pause subset; English full set 84.8%, AUC 0.932). This is in small internally validated samples (n=33 per language, nested LOO-CV, p.6) with other configurations lower (39-85%), no external validation and no specialist comparator. This matches the narrowed wording in the same way as P-77's best theme. CAVEATS for the record: (a) the in-band accuracy comes from one of seven feature subsets in one language, not a pre-specified model; the full feature set gives 75.8% (Hungarian) and 84.8% (English). (b) Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity are computed at the equal error rate, a threshold chosen on the pooled CV outputs (p.6), so they are optimistic; the AUCs (0.912/0.932) are threshold-free and consistent. (c) If admitted, the narrowed wording's parenthetical must add 'telephone-recorded speech in two memory-clinic samples (Szeged, New York)', and its 'other' range must widen to include near-chance subsets. INDEPENDENCE: distinct from I-CONECT (P-76/P-77) and the Memory Guard sample (P-101). No shared authors with the supporters or the other candidates (P-333, P-9, P-6). The Hungarian Szeged recordings belong to the same group's corpus family as P-59 (registry note; P-59 is neither a supporter nor a candidate here), and that family would count once. REGISTRY DEFECT: Best_Metric 'Acc 92' is not a printed accuracy; the highest accuracy is 90.9%, and 92.3% is the recall of that configuration (Table 3/4). Elsevier glyph note: the extract renders '=' as the character '¼' ('n ¼ 33') and drops en-dashes in ranges ('66.776.9%' = 66.7-76.9%); no verdict depends on this.

quotes.quote: During this process, one of the investigators was in the same room as the subject, while a second investigator called the subject on a mobile phone from another room. [...] Then, the second investigator introduced herself over the phone and asked the participant to talk about his or her previous day [...] Each participant’s monologue was recorded by a call recorder application installed on the mobile phone device.

Both the English-speaking (n ¼ 33; New York, NY, USA) and the Hungarian-speaking (n ¼ 33; Szeged, Hungary) participants were diagnosed as MCI or HC. This decision was based on Petersen’s criteria (Petersen et al., 1999) in both language groups

Having so few (i.e. n ¼ 33 for each language) examples, we did not create separate training and test sets, but opted for speaker-wise cross-validation (CV); that is, we always trained our SVM model on the features extracted from the speech of 32 speakers.

We calculated these values at Equal Error Rate (EER); that is, we chose the decision threshold between the posterior estimates of the two classes (provided by the SVM classiﬁer) in a way which minimizes the absolute difference between the scores sensitivity and speciﬁcity (i.e. recall).
Besides an accuracy score of 84.8%, the recall/sensitivity and speciﬁcity values were also around 85%.
Furthermore, the AUC and minCllr values are also quite good (0.932 and 0.305, respectively), indicating that the temporal parameters described in Table 2 allowed accurate MCI detection in this case.

However, ﬁller-related temporal parameters turned out to be surprisingly useful: besides an AUC value of 0.912 and a minCllr value of 0.200, we achieved classiﬁcation accuracy, recall (sensitivity) and speciﬁcity scores above 90%; with a precision score of 85.7%, it led to an F-measure value of 88.9.

Using all 15 temporal parameters led to a ﬁne performance, but exploiting the silent pause-related attributes was only scarcely better than simple guessing (AUC scores of 0.519 and 0.531, without and with the speech tempo-derived attributes, respectively).
while for Hungarian, the classiﬁcation performance was acceptable (with classiﬁcation metrics falling into the range 66.776.9% and with an AUC value of 0.727).
